summary.text: Electric charge is a property of matter that makes it feel a force in an electromagnetic field, and it comes in two kinds, positive and negative.
Like charges push apart and unlike charges pull together, while an object with no net charge is called neutral.
In ordinary matter electrons carry negative charge and protons carry positive charge, so an excess of either decides an object's overall charge.

facts.label: Unit
facts.value: The coulomb, named after Charles-Augustin de Coulomb

facts.label: Conservation
facts.value: Total charge in an isolated system never changes

facts.label: Franklin's rule
facts.value: Positive meant the charge on glass rubbed with silk

facts.label: Quark charges
facts.value: Fractions of e, but never found alone

items.prompt: You rub a balloon on your hair and the balloon ends up with a negative charge. What is true of your hair?

options.label: It is left with an equal amount of positive charge
It stays neutral, since only the balloon was changed
It gains the same negative charge as the balloon has
It loses its protons, which move over to the balloon

items.explain: Rubbing moves charge from one material to the other, leaving an opposite charge of the same size behind.

items.prompt: A neutral atom picks up one extra electron. What is it now?

options.label: A positive ion, because it has gained something
A negative ion, because electrons outnumber protons
Still a neutral atom, just a slightly heavier one
A new element, because its electron count changed

items.explain: With more electrons than protons the atom carries a net negative charge, which makes it a negative ion.

items.prompt: Two balloons each carry a negative charge and are hung close together. What do they do?

options.label: They drift together, since charged things attract
They ignore each other, as both are the same sort
They push away from each other
They swing together then spring apart repeatedly

items.explain: Charges of the same sign repel one another.

items.prompt: A scientist measures the charge on a tiny free-floating speck. Which total could it be, in units of the elementary charge?

options.label: One and a half units
A third of a unit
Two and a half units
Three whole units

items.explain: Free charges come only in whole multiples of the elementary charge.

items.prompt: Inside a sealed, insulated box you rub a glass rod with silk. Compared with before, what happens to the box's total charge?

options.label: It grows, since rubbing makes new charge
It shrinks, since some charge leaks into the air
It stays the same, as charge only shifts around
It doubles, since both objects become charged

items.explain: In an isolated system the total charge does not change; rubbing only moves charge between the objects.

items.prompt: Quarks carry fractions of the elementary charge. Why do we never see a lone object with a third of that charge?

options.label: Quarks only exist combined, in particles with whole-number charges
Fractional charge is too weak for any instrument to detect
Quarks cancel each other out and leave no charge at all
Quarks turn into electrons whenever they are separated

items.explain: Quarks are found only inside particles whose total charge is a whole multiple of e, and free quarks have never been seen.
